title: One invoice, new bank details
subtitle: Checked against the public record before paying
note: The plumbing firm and the invoice are a made-up example. The supplier is a real Swiss company checked on the public record on the date shown, under a made-up name, Aquorim AG, with its web addresses renamed to match. Every finding is an Antevo tool’s answer on that date.

tries.label: The invoice, line by line
tries.source: Antevo Guard and Antevo Companies, 25 Nov 2026. Three of Guard’s four sources answered.

items.name: The email address
evidence: The email came from aquorim-ch.com; the website the firm knows is aquorim.ch
The sender’s address differs by the added word “ch”

items.name: Is that address real?
evidence: aquorim-ch.com is not registered: its registry holds no record
The internet’s address book (DNS) does not know it

items.name: The new bank account
evidence: The account is in Lithuania, while the company is registered in Switzerland
Guard was given the two letters the account starts with, never the number

items.name: The company itself
evidence: Aquorim AG is on the Swiss company register, status “entered in the register”, canton of St. Gallen
Its website, aquorim.ch, was registered on 6 May 1996 and points to a web server
Not found on the US, EU, UK and Swiss sanctions lists under its name or its number

items.name: Not checked
evidence: The certificate logs did not answer in this check
A source that did not answer is not a clean result

items.do: Call the supplier on a number you already have
items.why: From an old invoice, a contract or your own contacts, never from the email. Ask one question: did your bank details change?

items.do: Compare the account with the last one you paid
items.why: Your own payment history shows it. A new country is worth that call on its own.

items.do: Read the sender’s address letter by letter
items.why: One added word, one swapped letter or a different ending is enough.

items.do: Look the company up in the official register
items.why: The register has the final word on the name, the seat and who may sign.

items.do: Already paid? Call your bank at once, then report it
items.why: The sooner the bank knows, the better the chance of stopping the transfer.

sections.title: Sanctions lists
sections.so_what: A look at four lists, not an official compliance check. It says nothing about who sent the email.
evidence: Not found under its name or its number on the US, EU, UK and Swiss lists, checked 25 Nov 2026
Not being found does not mean unrestricted: a company owned by a listed party can be restricted without being listed

sections.title: The register lately
sections.verdict: No change in the last 30 days
sections.so_what: The register does not hold bank details, so it cannot confirm the change or rule it out. It does show the company did not move or change its name in the weeks before the email.
evidence: Thirteen official notices since 2019
The latest on 16 December 2025
None in the 30 days before 25 November 2026
sections.source: Antevo Companies, official gazette notices, read 25 Nov 2026

sections.title: The same invoice, from a free email service
sections.so_what: A clean answer is not a green light. A careful fraud can pass every public check, which is why the phone call comes first.
evidence: Checked again as if the email came from a free webmail address and the account were Swiss
Guard notes the free email service
Nothing found that contradicts the public record in the four sources that answered

sections.title: What Guard does not see
sections.so_what: What settles an invoice like this is the supplier’s own answer, on a number you trust.
evidence: Guard reads public records about companies. It does not check people, who owns a bank account, or transactions, and it does not say whether a payment should be made.

links.text: The company is real and its record is quiet; the three things that do not match are all about the email and the account. The record describes the company, not who sent the invoice.
The lookalike only shows because the firm already knew the supplier’s real website. What you know about a supplier is the other half of every check.

watch: Any new invoice or email that says bank details have changed
The sender’s address on the next message from this supplier
New notices in the supplier’s register file
disclaimer: From Antevo answers on public records, each dated. Guard reads public records about companies. It does not check people, who owns a bank account, or transactions, and it does not say whether a payment should be made. A look at sanctions lists is not a compliance check. Not legal advice.
